title: Ten million downloads, eight days, one refusal — the first border for AI agents
deck: Meta launched its personal AI agent Muse in the UK on 24 November. Downloads passed 10 million after the US launch. Four UK regulators sent ministers a joint letter eight days earlier telling firms to talk to them before launch, and three of them issued statements on launch day. Meta declined the FCA's offer to test Muse together in its sandbox.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: Meta launched its personal AI agent Muse in the UK on 24 November 2026, the third market after the US (8 September) and Singapore (October). Reuters reported downloads passed 10 million after the US launch. Its 15 UK partners are retail and travel names, and payment runs through Stripe's Onelink and Shopify's Shop Pay.

Britain received personal AI agents without any pre-launch screening, relying on after-the-fact supervision under existing consumer and data law. The four DRCF chiefs sent ministers a joint letter on 16 November demanding risk assessment before launch while admitting that engagement had 'not been consistently early or open across the relevant regulators'. The CMA, ICO and FCA each issued a statement on launch day.

The FCA offered to test Muse together in its sandbox and Meta declined (WIRED, 26 November). The only control that worked before launch sat in the payment rail: Onelink issues an agent-only digital copy of the card and every purchase needs approval, and Meta published no spending-limit feature. Korea's FSC holds its first agentic payment meeting in early December, and 77.5% of card company staff surveyed said current law is insufficient.
body:
On 24 November 2026 Meta put its personal AI agent Muse on the UK market. Anyone aged 18 or over can use it free on the app, the web and WhatsApp. It is the third market after the US and Singapore, and Reuters reported that downloads passed 10 million after the US launch. Its UK partners are 15 retail and travel names including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury's, Ocado, Currys and ASOS.

![A humanoid assistant holding a single card walks alone through an immigration gate whose glass booth stands empty, three unopened envelopes on the counter](/assets/img/articles/muse-uk-launch-pre-approval-gap-2026.jpg)

## The letter that arrived eight days earlier

Britain has no procedure that screens a personal AI agent before launch. Regulators take the position that existing law already applies. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Ofcom said in a joint statement on 30 October that competition, consumer, data protection, financial and payments rules all apply to agents, and that an agent's autonomy does not reduce the responsibility of the organisation that deploys it. On 16 November the four chiefs sent a joint letter to four ministers demanding risk assessment and safeguards before launch. The letter carries one line of the regulators' own diagnosis.

> "Some firms have engaged early and constructively, but engagement has not been consistently early or open across the relevant regulators." — DRCF joint letter, 16 November 2026

## Three statements on launch day

Three statements came out in one day, 24 November. The CMA said it had been in talks for several weeks after Meta told it of the launch plans, and that the terms changed at the end of that. Meta must now exercise reasonable skill and care in providing Muse, and the terms acknowledge that outputs may still be inaccurate and that instructed actions may not be completed as intended. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold said Meta had agreed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme. In "Our approach to Agentic AI" the FCA wrote that calling itself a technology company does not let a firm escape authorisation, and that payments, financial promotions, credit broking and advice can require it. The UK version of Muse, unlike the US one, does not reach bank, investment or loan data. Meta said it will connect banking services once it holds the licences.

## The one that was declined in the sandbox

The most concrete scene came from WIRED on 26 November. Colin Payne, the FCA's head of innovation, said the FCA proposed testing Muse together in its sandbox and Meta declined. Meta told the FCA of its plans only last month, he said, and designing such a test normally takes weeks to months. Agents are hitting the streets and most of them come from the US, he said, and if Muse is as widely used in Britain the regulator needs to see what it does. Meta would only say that it has engaged constructively with regulators.

## The only control was at the checkout

The one control that worked before launch sat at the payment step. Payment runs through Stripe's Onelink, which issues a digital copy of the user's card that only agents using that wallet can open. Every purchase needs approval, the model cannot see passwords or card details, and a separate security agent checks actions against the permissions granted. Meta has published no UK user numbers and no spending-limit feature. The FCA told regulated firms to consider whether to accept payments instructed by an agent or from an agent-controlled wallet. Instead of authorisation and review, one card and an approval button held the line.

## Korea's door opens in December

In Korea the discussion is only starting. The Financial Services Commission will bring fintechs and banks to the Korea Financial Telecommunications and Clearings Institute in Seoul in early December for its first agentic payment meeting. FSC chairman Lee Eok-won may attend. The agenda is identity verification for agents, extra approval steps, protection of personal and payment data, and who is liable for wrong or unauthorised payments. BC Card signed a memorandum with Pickle, a personal AI agent startup, on 18 November to run staged technical validation. Pickle passed 200,000 monthly users within a month of its beta. The industry's own diagnosis is colder. In a survey of 71 card company staff presented at a credit finance forum on 24 November, 80.3% expected agentic payments within five years and 77.5% said current law is insufficient; the biggest risk they named was not technology but unclear liability.

## Not a country without a check, but one where the check comes later

Britain did not remove the check; it moved it after the fact. What exists before launch is a letter, existing law and one card at the checkout, and in that structure the first test bench is a complaints form. The CMA opened a form for people to report their experience with Muse and other agents, and guidance it issued with the ICO tells users to start with the most limited mode. Korea will draw the blueprint for the same window at its December meeting. The question is not whether to screen the agent but what to leave on the record. The scope and duration of the mandate, the unit of approval and who pays when something goes wrong all have to be in the table before any after-the-fact review can work. The sentence the DRCF left in October is the first row of that table: an agent's autonomy does not reduce the responsibility of the organisation that deploys it.

factCheck.title: Fact check & sources
factCheck.note: The statement that Britain has no pre-launch authorisation or screening for personal AI agents is a description of the structure based on the regulators' own documents. The DRCF and the four regulators said existing law already applies, and no material showing a pre-launch review was found. The refusal of the FCA sandbox joint test is not an FCA publication but WIRED's account of remarks by Colin Payne, the FCA's head of innovation; Meta answered only that it has engaged constructively with the appropriate regulators. The 10 million downloads is Reuters' figure, while WIRED says more than 10 million people in North America set up Muse, which is a different measure. Reports citing Meta's announcement differ between 14 and 15 UK partners; this article follows the 15-name list that includes Cult Beauty. Meta's own announcement page returned 403 when opened, so the partner list, the Onelink description and the purchase-approval design were cross-checked through secondary reports (FashionUnited, Agentic Commerce Atlas, MacRumors, Home of Direct Commerce). The professional diligence wording and the acknowledgement that outputs may be inaccurate are as WIRED quoted the UK and EU terms. Every Korean figure is from press reports. The date and attendees of the FSC's December meeting are not a confirmed announcement but the Maeil Business Newspaper's account citing industry officials, and the chairman's attendance is under consideration. The BC Card and Pickle tie-up is a memorandum, not a launched service. The survey of 71 card company staff was the Credit Finance Research Institute's own poll presented at the forum.

title: Anatomy of Dominance 58.8% — The space left by Bitcoin was filled by the dollar, not alts
deck: Bitcoin dominance fell from 60.61% on November 12 to 58.76% on the 26th. During the same period, the altcoin season index rose from 49 to 58, but is 17 points short of the baseline of 75. If you follow where the proportion has shifted, you will find stablecoins, not Ethereum or altcoins.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: Bitcoin dominance fell from 60.61% on November 12 to 58.76% on the 26th. Based on CoinMarketCap, it was 59.3% on November 17th, 58.6% on the 24th, and 58.5% on the 25th. Depending on the provider, the 26th value varies from 57.3 to 58.8%.

The altcoin season index is 49 on the 17th, 58 on the 24th, 52 on the 25th, and 58 on the 26th. Above 75 is alt season and below 25 is Bitcoin season, so 58 is a neutral range. The highest this year was 64 on September 27th.

During the same period, the 0.7% point decrease in the proportion of Bitcoin went not to Ethereum (10.1% → 10.0%) but to others, including stablecoins (30.6% → 31.4%). On the 24th, there was a net outflow of $521.5 million from the U.S. Bitcoin and Ethereum spot ETF.
body:
On the evening of November 26, the most cited number in the virtual asset market was not the price of Bitcoin, but its share. Bitcoin dominance fell to the 58% range, and the altcoin season index pointed to 58. If you put the two numbers side by side, it reads like a textbook signal of an ‘altcoin market turn’. However, the fund flow at the same time tells a different story.

![Bitcoin dominance fell from 60.61% on November 12 to 58.76% on the 26th, and the alt season index fell below 75.](/assets/img/articles/btc-dominance-58-altseason-index-2026.jpg)

## From 60.61% to 58.76%

Bitcoin dominance is the proportion of Bitcoin in the total virtual asset market capitalization. Crypto Briefing reported on November 25 that Dominance peaked at 60.61% on November 12 and then fell below 60%, and that the aggregate figure on the 25th was 57.3-58.5% depending on the provider. Token Post's weekly values ​​citing CoinMarketCap statistics are 59.3% on the 17th (60.3% the previous week), 58.6% on the 24th (59.4% the previous week), and 58.5% on the 25th.

Share moves differently from price. If other assets decrease faster in the overall market capitalization, which is the denominator, the proportion of Bitcoin will increase even if it remains in place, and if Bitcoin falls first, the proportion will fall. November was the latter. Bitcoin fell 51.8% from its all-time high of $126,198 on October 6, 2025, to $60,800 on the 26th, and the 4th quarter return was -29.3% as of the 25th, the second worst quarter after the 4th quarter of 2018 (-43.51%). Ethereum -5.6% and Solana -4.7% also fell (7-day return as of the 26th).

## Alt season index 58, baseline 75

The Altcoin Season Index is the percentage of assets that have yielded higher returns than Bitcoin among the top 100 altcoins (excluding stablecoins) by market capitalization over the past 90 days. If it is above 75, it is classified as alt season, and if it is below 25, it is classified as Bitcoin season. According to Token Post, it was 49 on November 17th, 58 on the 24th, 52 on the 25th, and 58 on the 26th. The highest in 2026 was 64 on September 27, and the lowest was 14 on December 19, 2025.

The number refers to ‘neutral’ rather than ‘all-time high’. An index of 58 does not mean that 58% of altcoins have risen, but that more than half of them have surpassed Bitcoin in a 90-day return comparison.

## Where the importance has shifted

The weekly composition reported by Token Post as compiled by CoinMarketCap is as follows. It changed from Bitcoin 59.3%, Ethereum 10.1%, and other 30.6% on November 17 to Bitcoin 58.6%, Ethereum 10.0%, and other 31.4% on the 24th. Ethereum did not take the 0.7% point that Bitcoin gave. The ones that have increased are others, including stable coins.

In the same report, Crypto Briefing explained that Tether (USDT) dominance moved in the 8-14% range, and that the proportion of dollar-linked assets naturally increases when the price is falling. According to the Glassnode tally reported by Block Media on November 19, stablecoin supply decreased by $14.2 billion in the 30 days ending November 9, recording the largest decrease since June 2022. This means that the proportion has increased but the supply has decreased, which is far from the picture of new funds flowing into altcoins.

|Classification|November 17|November 24|Altjang conditions|Judgment|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Bitcoin Dominance|59.3%|58.6%|Downtrend|meets|
|Ethereum Dominance|10.1%|10.0%|Rise|Not met|
|Others (including stablecoins)|30.6%|31.4%|Expanding focus on altcoins|Not met|
|Alt Season Index|49|58|75 or higher|Not met|

## Confirmed and unconfirmed

There are three confirmed facts. First, dominance peaked in mid-November and the difference between providers is around 1%p. Second, the alt-season index remains in the neutral range. Third, funds continued to flow out of the U.S. Bitcoin and Ethereum spot ETFs. The daily net outflow on the 24th, reported by Block Media as compiled by Farside Investors on November 26, was $453 million for Bitcoin and $521.5 million including Ethereum, and the Bitcoin ETF was in negative territory for 7 consecutive trading days.

What has not been confirmed is the direction of next month. The Federal Reserve will decide interest rates at its meeting on December 10. On November 23, The Bull Signal reported that the CME futures market was 100% reflecting the December hike, but this was a market expectation and not a decision. In its report on November 25, Galaxy Research maintained its previous judgment that if the June low (closing price of $58,525) breaks, it will go to a lower low.

The judgment of determining the proportion of altcoins based on dominance alone has little basis. When looking at Bitcoin dominance, USDT dominance, alt season index, stablecoin supply, and ETF funds together, as of November 26, only one of the five items met the 'alt market' condition.

factCheck.title: Fact check & sources
factCheck.note: Dominance varies by about 1%p depending on the provider and time of aggregation (57.3-58.8% on the 26th). The main text separates the Coin Market Cap series (Token Post report) and the Crypto Briefing citation range, and does not compare the values ​​of different providers as one continuous time series. The interpretation that 'dominance decline = alt market' is based on the definition that dominance is a relative ratio and the three indicators of USDT dominance, stablecoin supply, and ETF funds, and does not recommend buying or selling specific altcoins. The FOMC results on December 10th and the timing of the alt market switch have not been confirmed.

title: Ten weeks become thirty, six months become thirty — the AI build-out queues in three layers
deck: In the 2026 semiconductor supply chain survey by SEMI and McKinsey, substrate material lead times went from 10 weeks to 30 and assembly and packaging equipment from 23 weeks to 37. In the substrate chain some processing equipment now takes 30 months after a purchase order instead of six, and the Japanese precision parts inside that equipment take half a year. Samsung Electro-Mechanics' new Sejong line, backed by 6.78 trillion won, starts mass production in September 2028.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: In the semiconductor supply chain survey SEMI and McKinsey presented on November 17, 2026, average lead times ran 16.4 weeks, 27% above normal. Substrate materials that were normal a year earlier went from 10 weeks to 30, assembly and packaging equipment from 23 to 37 weeks (61%), and chemicals and process materials from 10 to 17 weeks (70%).

In the substrate industry, lead times for some FC-BGA bonding, cutting and metallization equipment have stretched from about six months after a purchase order to 30 months (not the average across all such equipment), and the Japanese precision motors, servos and drivers inside it take half a year. Samsung Electro-Mechanics' CCL and PPG purchase prices rose 26.0% in the first nine months and its substrate selling prices 28.1%.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics will start its new Sejong line in September 2028 and its Vietnam plant in June 2030 on a 6.78 trillion won investment. Intel has committed $5.3bn to $6.1bn to secure substrates, Counterpoint sees a 20% shortfall around 2027, and order backlogs at Korean PCB makers rose 22% to 115% quarter on quarter.
body:
In September 2026 Samsung Electro-Mechanics decided to put 4.27 trillion won into its Sejong plant and 2.51 trillion won into its Vietnam subsidiary, 6.78 trillion won in all, into FC-BGA substrates. The new Sejong line starts mass production in September 2028 and Vietnam in June 2030. The numbers that make that timetable worth reading again came out on November 25 and 26.

![At the end of a production line stacked with substrates, a robotic arm is handed a single small motor, and behind it a calendar unrolls toward 2028](/assets/img/articles/fcbga-equipment-lead-time-30-months-2026.jpg)

## The clock on materials — ten weeks become thirty

The 2026 semiconductor supply chain survey that SEMI and McKinsey presented in a webinar on November 17 drew more than 200 responses from materials and equipment suppliers, device makers and OSATs. Average lead times across the global chain run 16.4 weeks, 27% above normal. Substrates stand out. Substrate material lead times, normal in last year's survey, tripled from 10 weeks to 30. Assembly and packaging equipment went from 23 weeks to 37 (61%), and chemicals and process materials from 10 to 17 (70%). 82% of respondents said demand rose year on year, and 42% of materials suppliers and 38% of equipment suppliers reported longer lead times than in the previous quarter. In the same survey 88% of suppliers expect revenue growth over the next 12 months. Demand has come back broadly, yet only leading-edge capacity is stretched to its limit while inventories pile up downstream. Substrates jam first for a structural reason. A substrate carries electrical signals between the chip and the mainboard, and the ones inside AI accelerators and server CPUs are larger and carry more circuit layers than those for ordinary IT gear, so the same plant yields fewer of them.

## The clock on equipment — six months become thirty

The front-page story Electronic Times ran on November 26 shows the bottleneck moving one layer further in. Some of the bonding, cutting and metallization equipment for FC-BGA substrates that arrived six months after a purchase order now takes 30 months. Large substrate makers are paying in advance to ask for faster delivery, and some send letters of intent before a formal order to hold capacity. Equipment makers say that even with more orders they lack the parts to ship on time. The stretch began with semiconductor manufacturing equipment, where deliveries now run as long as three years, and spread to substrates. The 30 months applies to some equipment, not to FC-BGA equipment as a whole.

## The end of the queue — a Japanese motor that takes six months

The companies that build the equipment stand in the same line. The more advanced the tool, the more it depends on Japanese parts, and capacity is short for precision stage motors, servo motors, drivers and controllers. A Japanese part that used to be available immediately now takes about half a year, according to the head of an FC-BGA bonding equipment maker. The FC-BGA market is led by Japan's Ibiden and Shinko Electric and Taiwan's Unimicron, with Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Daeduck Electronics and LG Innotek pushing in from Korea. Materials are not far away either: the CCL and PPG supply lines named in Samsung Electro-Mechanics' third-quarter report are Japan's Resonac and Mitsubishi.

## The numbers that reached the cost sheet first

Price has already reached the cost sheet. Samsung Electro-Mechanics' average CCL and PPG purchase price for the first nine months of 2026 is up 26.0% from a year earlier, while the average selling price of its semiconductor package substrates rose 28.1%. LG Innotek's substrate material purchase price rose 13.7%, after 15.0% last year. Substrate raw material inventory grew 53.2% at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, from 66.7 billion won to 102.2 billion won, and 14.6% at LG Innotek, from 34.6 billion to 39.6 billion won. TrendForce put the lead time for ABF substrates in the second week of November at 48 to 56 weeks, up to 4.7 times the balanced level of 12 weeks. Samsung Electro-Mechanics says it is negotiating selling prices to reflect higher material costs and tight supply, and some customers are helping fund substrate makers' capacity and guaranteeing long-term volumes.

## Not the money announced but the date the tools arrive

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' package solution division posted 2.4357 trillion won in sales for the first nine months, up 47% from a year earlier, and its operating margin rose from 5.3% to 15.2%. Even so, the company said this on its third-quarter earnings call.

> "Even with this large expansion it is hard to meet all customer demand, and requests for more volume keep coming." — Samsung Electro-Mechanics, third-quarter earnings call

Intel said in its third-quarter filing that it cannot adequately meet data-center CPU demand because packaging substrates are scarce, and it has signed two substrate supply contracts since the quarter closed. Expected spending is $5.3bn to $6.1bn, 7.1 to 8.2 trillion won. Counterpoint Research expects the shortfall in high-performance substrates to reach 20% around 2027. Order backlogs at Korean PCB makers rose 22% to 115% quarter on quarter, according to Hana Securities; the list includes Simmtech, Daeduck Electronics, Korea Circuit and Isu Petasys. LG Innotek's package solution sales came to 481.8 billion won in the third quarter, up 10.1%, and the industry expects it to close long-term supply agreements with three North American chipmakers as it moves into high-end AI accelerator and server substrates by 2028. Demand is arriving in Korea, but the calendar for the tools and parts that would serve it points at 2028 and 2030. The two to four years between the start of that capacity and the 2027 peak of the shortfall belong to these companies. What separates results in the next cycle is not the size of the investment announced but the schedule for when the equipment comes in.

factCheck.title: Fact check & sources
factCheck.note: The 30 months refers to some, not all, of the bonding, cutting and metallization equipment for FC-BGA substrates: Electronic Times called it 'nearly five times the usual level', and TokenPost noted that it is not the average across FC-BGA equipment. This article keeps that limit. The 30 months for finished equipment and the half year for the Japanese parts inside it are different measurements of different things. The item-level lead times (16.4 weeks on average, substrate materials 10 to 30 weeks, assembly and packaging equipment 23 to 37 weeks, chemicals and process materials 10 to 17 weeks, 82% seeing higher demand, 42% of materials and 38% of equipment suppliers reporting longer lead times) are News Tomato's reading of the SEMI and McKinsey 2026 semiconductor supply chain survey; what SEMI's own survey page states directly is 200-plus respondents, lead times 27% above historical norms, 88% of suppliers expecting revenue growth over 12 months, and leading-edge capacity at its limit while downstream inventories pile up. The full survey report was not examined. Samsung Electro-Mechanics' 26.0% (CCL and PPG purchase price), 28.1% (package substrate selling price) and 2.4357 trillion won in nine-month package solution sales were read from the published quarterly report, while LG Innotek's 13.7% and the raw material inventory figures (Samsung Electro-Mechanics 66.7bn to 102.2bn won, LG Innotek 34.6bn to 39.6bn won) are as News Tomato cited them from both companies' quarterly reports and were not checked against the originals. Intel's $5.3bn to $6.1bn is the expected outlay for two substrate supply contracts signed after the third quarter closed, of which $3.3bn is due by the end of 2027. Counterpoint's 20% is a forecast for around 2027. The September 2028 start at Sejong and June 2030 at Vietnam follow the JoongAng Ilbo report; News Tomato writes 'gradual mass production from next year', so the timing is reported differently. Hana Securities' 22% to 115% backlog growth is as reported by Yonhap from the brokerage note.

title: The application says 500 million tonnes. The announcement has no number — what holds nickel at $15,000 is 79,266 tonnes in Busan and Gwangyang
deck: Indonesian miners applied to dig more than 500 million wet tonnes in 2027, and the government closed applications on 15 November without publishing a figure. A quota cuts ore, not refined nickel, because smelters import Philippine ore. LME three-month nickel fell from $16,230 on 13 November to $15,210 on 25 November, and 79,266 tonnes of the 275,604 tonnes in LME warehouses sit in Busan and Gwangyang.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: Indonesia closed applications for its 2027 nickel ore quota (RKAB) on 15 November but had published no figure by 24 November. Miners applied for more than 500 million wet tonnes, and the 2026 quota itself was raised during the year from 260-270 million to 290-300 million tonnes.

The quota sets how much ore mines dig, not how much nickel smelters produce. Smelters covered the gap by importing 65% more Philippine ore in the first half, and 750,000 tonnes of LME and SHFE stock — about 11 weeks of consumption — keeps the price near $15,000. The INSG sees a 70,000-tonne surplus in 2027.

Of the 275,604 tonnes of nickel in LME warehouses, 79,266 tonnes (28.8%) are in Busan and Gwangyang. Korea's ferronickel imports from Indonesia rose from about 34,000 tonnes in 2022 to about 172,000 tonnes in 2025, and POSCO and LX International hold stakes in Indonesian smelting and mining.
body:
On 13 November the official LME settlement for three-month nickel was $16,230 a tonne. On 25 November it was $15,210: $1,020, or 6.3%, gone in twelve days. Indonesia's signals of output cuts do not explain a fall that size. Over the same period nickel in LME warehouses rose from 272,724 to 275,604 tonnes.

![A nickel warehouse at Busan port before dawn: grey nickel briquettes stacked on pallets beside steel drums, a forklift, and a container terminal and bulk carrier in the mist beyond the open shutter. Image · AI illustration](/assets/img/articles/nickel-quota-2027-korea-warehouse-2026.jpg)

## The application says 500 million tonnes. The announcement has no number

Indonesia sets each mine's output every year through its work plan and budget, the RKAB. Applications for 2027 closed on 15 November, and according to market analysis miners applied for more than 500 million wet tonnes (wmt). By 24 November the government had published no 2027 quota figure.

On 2 November Bahlil Lahadalia, coordinating minister for energy and investment, said supply running past global demand of about 3.5 million tonnes a year had pushed the price below $16,000, to about $15,800, and that he would tighten it through the quota. Tri Winarno, director general of minerals and coal, said the 2027 figure would come in below the revised 2026 quota of 290-300 million tonnes. That 2026 quota had itself started at 260-270 million tonnes and was raised to 290-300 million during the year.

## The benchmark reflects the price before the rally

The nickel benchmark (HMA) that the energy ministry applies from 15 to 30 November is $15,596.88 a tonne. It is up 0.76% on the previous half-month, but the number averages LME prices from 19 October to 9 November, so the late-November decline has not reached it yet.

## The quota cuts ore, not refined nickel

The RKAB decides how much ore mines dig. It does not decide how much ferronickel, nickel matte or MHP smelters make. The Indonesian Nickel Smelters Forum (FINI) estimated that smelters need 340-350 million tonnes a year to run at 90% utilisation, while the 2026 quota was roughly 100 million tonnes short of that. The gap is filled two ways: domestic ore prices rise, and imports arrive. Indonesian imports of Philippine nickel ore rose 65% in the first half, and FINI expects Philippine imports to reach 30 million tonnes in 2026.

> "Do they want to cut world supply, or cut the RKAB? If you cut the RKAB, does world supply necessarily fall? No. Because they can import." — Agus Superiadi, at an Eramet briefing in Jakarta, 25 November

A senior nickel mining adviser, he said tightening the quota only lifts domestic ore prices and squeezes smelter costs while refined nickel reaching the world market does not fall, so the rally does not hold. To cut supply you have to cut smelter output, not mine permits. Reports in early November said Huayou, Tsingshan and other major producers were considering output cuts of up to 50%.

## What holds the price is eleven weeks of stock

The world consumes about 3.5 million tonnes of nickel a year. Stock in LME and Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) warehouses alone comes to about 750,000 tonnes, eleven weeks of it. LME warehouses hold 275,604 tonnes, and on 25 November cash metal traded $175 below the three-month contract, a contango that has run for more than 28 sessions. Metal for immediate use is plentiful; metal for later delivery costs more. The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) has moved its 2026 forecast from a 32,000-tonne deficit in April to a 19,000-tonne surplus, and sees a 70,000-tonne surplus in 2027.

## One tonne in every four of LME nickel sits in Busan and Gwangyang

The LME warehouse report of 23 November shows 79,266 of 275,604 tonnes (28.8%) in Korea, second only to Singapore's 85,560 tonnes (31.0%), with Taiwan next at 63,546 tonnes (23.1%). Inside Korea the metal is split between Busan and Gwangyang. In the month since 23 October the Korean total fell by 198 tonnes. At the 25 November cash price of $15,035 a tonne and a reference rate of 1,343.60 won to the dollar, that is about 1.6 trillion won of metal sitting still.

## Raw material from Indonesia, stock in Korea

Korea's ferronickel imports from Indonesia rose fivefold, from about 34,000 tonnes in 2022 to about 172,000 tonnes in 2025. POSCO Holdings owns 49% of the smelter PT Nikol Metal Industry, and LX International owns 69.57% of the mine operator PT Adhi Kartiko Pratama. When the quota tightens, output at those mines is restricted first, and the higher domestic ore price eats into smelting margins. The 79,266 tonnes in Korean warehouses, by contrast, are waiting for the price to rise.

## Two numbers due in December

One is the 2027 RKAB quota. The other is the European Commission's verdict on Anglo American's sale of its Brazilian nickel business to China's MMG, a deal worth up to $500 million. The commission has said it will finish its Phase II review by 21 December, and European steelmakers are asking for annual deliveries to Europe of 11,500-16,000 tonnes as a condition. If the deal is blocked, 39,700 tonnes of Brazilian ferronickel could leave the market.

If the quota comes in below 290 million tonnes the price will react first. But for a rally to last past three days, the 275,604 tonnes in LME warehouses, Busan and Gwangyang included, have to fall. That is why the price still looks at the warehouse on the day December's number lands.

factCheck.title: Fact check & sources
factCheck.note: Prices follow the LME official settlement prices (cash and three-month) and the daily stocks published by Westmetall. For 25 November the three-month contract shows three different numbers — $15,210 as official settlement, $15,169 as the LME closing price and $15,270 in overnight electronic trading — and the text uses the official settlement only. The fall of $1,020, or 6.3%, from $16,230 on 13 November to $15,210 on 25 November is our calculation from those two values. SMM and Kalkine reported $16,462–16,525 in electronic and intraday trading in mid-November, but the official settlements of 15,990 on 17 November and 15,985 on 18 November did not hold that level, so the text describes only a move that did not last three days. The 2027 application volume of 'more than 500 million wet tonnes' comes from market analysis (Discovery Alert, 24 November) quoting officials and is not an ESDM statistic. The 2026 quota was reported by S&P Global on 2 November as 260–270 million tonnes initially and 290–300 million tonnes revised, while SMM put the revision at about 295–300 million wmt. KOTRA's Surabaya office, by contrast, described in July a cut from 379 million tonnes to about 250 million (−34%), which does not reconcile; the figures differ in date and scope, so the text uses the November reports. The 'roughly 100 million tonnes' gap between smelter requirements and the quota is our comparison of the FINI figure (quoted by KOTRA, against a 250–260 million tonne quota) with the November quota. Minister Bahlil's '2.5 million tonnes above market need' refers to supply capacity, not to the 750,000 tonnes in LME and SHFE stocks or to the INSG's 19,000 tonnes, and the text does not use it; only global demand of 3.5 million tonnes is quoted. The INSG forecasts are as reported by Kontan on 21 November (a 19,000-tonne surplus in 2026 and 70,000 tonnes in 2027), and the 32,000-tonne deficit is the April INSG forecast cited by KOTRA. 'Eleven weeks' is 750,000 tonnes divided by annual consumption of 3.5 million tonnes. The $175 contango is $15,210 minus $15,035; SMM put the same day's LME 0-3 spread at −$169.61, a difference in valuation time. The country breakdown of LME stocks is The Vault Report's summary of the LME daily warehouse report of 23 November and was not checked against the LME's own spreadsheet; Busan and Gwangyang come from the LME's list of Korean locations, and the November 2026 split between the two is not confirmed. 79,266 tonnes × $15,035 a tonne × 1,343.60 won comes to about 1.6013 trillion won, before freight, storage and premiums. The ferronickel figures of 34,000 and 172,000 tonnes are the Climate Justice Centre (Ark) analysis of Korea Customs K-STAT data; ferronickel falls under HS 7202 (ferro-alloys), not HS 75 (nickel), and the figures are not converted to nickel content. Huayou's and Tsingshan's cuts of up to 50% are at the 'considering' stage as reported by SMM, not confirmed. The 39,700 tonnes of Brazilian ferronickel is Kalkine's figure and its source was not checked. The Anglo American–MMG deal carries conditions — up to $500 million, a Commission decision due on 21 December, a long-stop date of 31 December and increased European supply of 11,500–16,000 tonnes — and approval has not been decided.

title: No standard requires the mat to switch itself off — 2,354 fires in five years, 37 deaths
deck: Fires from electric heating mats and electric heaters killed 37 people and injured 219 in five years, 2,354 fires in all. Of the 532 mat fires attributed to carelessness, 87% were recorded as 'use or installation'. Yet safety standard KC 60335-2-17 fixes the heating wire and surface temperatures in numbers and does not require a device that cuts the power after a set time. After certification, the only window onto whether a product is still the product that was certified is the market survey each winter — and every year electric underblankets and mats are caught in it.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: Fires involving electric heating mats (electric blankets and seat cushions included) and electric heaters totalled 2,354 between 2021 and 2025, with 37 deaths and 219 injuries, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety said on Nov 18, 2026. Of the 532 mat fires blamed on carelessness, 461 (87%) were recorded as careless use or installation. The same notice advises using a timer — a sentence left to the user, not a condition on the product.

Safety standard KC 60335-2-17 sets temperature limits (95℃ for the heating wire, 37℃ for the sleeping surface) but has no clause requiring the appliance to switch itself off after a set time; the word 'timer' does not appear in its text. Post-certification checks are a periodic inspection every two years under Article 7 of the Electrical Appliances and Consumer Products Safety Control Act, plus a survey of products on sale.

A 2022 study by Korea Electrical Safety Corporation researchers found 294 of 1,308 mat fires (22.5%) had been concluded as carelessness from combustibles left nearby, a category that can absorb a failed temperature controller. Of ten certified products bought online, seven exceeded the surface temperature limit and three had controllers whose parts differed from the certified version. KATS ordered recalls of 76 mat products from 53 companies between 2014 and 2020, and five of the 12 electrical products recalled on Dec 11, 2025 were underblankets, seat cushions or mats.
body:
The conclusion first. **An electric heating mat does not switch itself off as the night goes on.** Safety standard KC 60335-2-17 contains one clause about time (22.110): if a control is set so that the appliance drops from high output to low output after a period, it must not switch itself back to high output. That is a condition on a device that already exists. No clause requires such a device, and the word 'timer' does not appear anywhere in the text of the standard.

The numbers the Ministry of the Interior and Safety released on Nov 18, 2026 read like this. Between 2021 and 2025 there were 2,354 fires involving electric heating mats (electric blankets and seat cushions included) and electric heaters (fan heaters and stoves), with 37 deaths and 219 injuries. Of the 532 mat fires attributed to carelessness, 461 — 87% — were careless use or installation. The same day's notice advises: 'use the timer function so the power turns off after a set time.' A sentence left to the user, not a condition on the product.

## The statistics that put people at the centre

In the 2010-2019 figures the National Fire Agency released in November 2020, electric mat fires numbered 2,443 and 47 people died. The causes were electrical factors at 50.1% and carelessness at 19.4%.

Recent figures reverse the order. Mat fires rose from 179 in 2021 to 243 in 2022 and 257 in 2023, the ministry reported in November 2024, and carelessness was the largest cause at 44%. Careless use or installation alone went from 54 cases to 102 and then 94, nearly double the 2021 level.

The two series cover different periods and classify causes differently, so they cannot be set side by side. What is clear is that in the recent figures the cause lands on the person, not the product.

## What the 87% can cover

An analysis published in 2022 in Fire Science and Engineering by researchers at the Korea Electrical Safety Corporation's Electrical Safety Research Institute looks again at that 87%. Reading the fire investigation reports for 1,308 mat fires between 2016 and 2020, they found 1,026 fires confined to the point of ignition, 506 of them localised. Of those 506, in 294 cases (22.5%) the burning was limited to the mat with no electrical traces such as melted insulation, and the cause was concluded as carelessness from combustibles left too close.

> > If a defective product whose temperature control had failed was in use, and only part of the combustibles charred with no other peculiarity visible, an investigator would probably have judged it a heat-accumulation fire and concluded carelessness from combustibles left nearby, the authors write.

A heat-accumulation fire under a duvet and a fire from a failed controller that kept the wire heating leave similar traces, and in the statistics they fall into the same box.

## Seven of ten certified products

The same paper re-tested ten safety-certified mats bought online against KC 60335-2-17. Seven exceeded the surface temperature limit (37℃, 45℃ at the foot end), one reaching 64.3℃. One exceeded the 95℃ limit for the heating wire at 96.1℃, and four exceeded the rated power tolerance of +10%, by up to +66.7%. Compared with the controllers as certified, three differed: current fuses, capacitors and SCRs had been changed.

Some products were caught in market surveys. KATS ran five safety investigations of electric mats — 2014, 2016, 2018, 2019 and 2020 — and ordered recalls of 76 products from 53 companies (8 underblankets, 52 mats, 16 floor mats). Temperature-rise failures were the largest defect category at 63 cases (86.3%). At the time of the study, recalled products were still on sale in 3 of 10 traditional market shops and on secondhand trading sites.

## The list that comes out in December

Last December 11 followed the same pattern. KATS examined 1,119 products across 54 winter items and ordered 53 recalls; five of the 12 electrical products were heating products. Two underblankets had heating wires at 113.5℃ and 108.8℃ (limit 95℃), two seat cushions had surfaces at 66.3℃ (limit 50℃) and 57.1℃, and one mat measured 110.0℃. The 2022 winter survey also recalled 12 mats, floor mats and cushions that exceeded temperature-rise limits.

![An electric mat left switched on under a folded duvet, its plug in the wall socket, a small controller resting beside it](/assets/img/articles/electric-mat-auto-off-standard-gap.jpg)

## The window the system has

Electric blankets, mats and electric beds are subject to safety certification (Annex 3 of the Enforcement Rules of the Electrical Appliances and Consumer Products Safety Control Act). Certification covers product testing and a factory inspection together (Article 2, subparagraph 5), and after certification the product faces a periodic inspection every two years, with self-inspection records kept for each product (Article 7).

The tests are not light. The controller runs 100,000 operations and the self-resetting overheating device 10,000 (24.1.4); there is a 500-hour temperature-rise test, and abnormal-operation tests with the pad folded in three layers (19.110) and the heating wire bunched (19.113). The temperature limits are numbers too: 95℃ for the wire insulation, 50℃ on a pad surface (85℃ for up to two hours), and for blankets and mattresses, in sleeping conditions, 60℃ in the first hour and afterwards 45℃ in the third nearest the foot end and 37℃ over the rest (11.101).

There are marking duties as well: underblankets must carry the 'do not use folded or creased' mark, the manual and product a low-temperature burn warning, and the control a manual switch and an off indication (Article 7, 22.112). What is missing is time. The standard fixes temperature and leaves time to the user.

## The same mat, a different door

A water-heating electric mat sits in a different tier. It is subject to safety confirmation, which needs a test by a testing body and a report to the authorities, without a factory inspection or a periodic inspection (Annex 4, Article 15). Of the 4,154 heating-product accidents the Korea Consumer Agency recorded between 2020 and 2024, water mats accounted for 684, and 415 of those (60.7%) involved product defects — the highest share of any item. A lower tier does not by itself prove more accidents; the count rests on hospital and fire station reports. But the item with the most complaints of defect sits in the tier with no factory inspection, and that is simply the number.

## One line left

Five years of statistics point 87% of the blame at a person's hand, and the safety standard fixes temperature but not time. The window onto whether a product is still what was certified is the market survey held each winter, and in it a few underblankets and mats are caught every year.

Three things can be done at home. Check the KC certification number on the label against the recall list at the Product Safety Information Center; store the mat rolled, not folded; do not layer it under a latex mattress or a heavy duvet. For sleeping, a surface temperature of 37℃ or below is advised.

This article reports only what could be verified against the text of the standards, government releases, academic papers and recall notices. When the two statistical series changed their classification, and how many recalled products were actually recovered, could not be confirmed.

title: 3.25% does not arrive today — December 15 at 3 p.m., and then your own reset date
deck: The Bank of Korea raised its policy rate from 3.00% to 3.25%. But the day an existing variable-rate borrower feels that decision is not today. The bank's funding cost enters the benchmark index through a Dec 15 disclosure, and a borrower's rate is recalculated only when the reset date written into the contract comes around. In the meantime, the five-year fixed rate has fallen below the variable rate.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: The Monetary Policy Committee raised the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25% on Nov 26 in a 5-2 vote, with members Hwang Kun-il and Lee Soo-hyung preferring a hold. The 2026 growth forecast rose to 3.9% and the 2027 forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%.

COFIX, the benchmark for variable-rate mortgages, rose 0.44 percentage points in two months to 3.62% for October. As of Nov 26 the five major banks' variable rates (4.52-6.59%) are above their five-year fixed rates (4.33-6.30%).

When a rate hike reaches an existing loan depends on which benchmark the contract names and on the reset cycle. November's COFIX is published on Dec 15. On a 300 million won loan at 5.0%, each 0.25 percentage point adds 750,000 won a year.
body:
At 10 a.m. on Nov 26, 2026, the Bank of Korea's Monetary Policy Committee raised the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25% from 3.00%. It is the third increase this year and a resumption three months after last month's unanimous hold. Yet the interest a variable-rate mortgage borrower pays tonight is the same as yesterday. Between the day the policy rate moves and the day the figure in the account changes sit two gates: the bank's funding cost and the reset date written into the contract.

![On a desk, a red pen circles one day on a year-end calendar beside a blurred loan agreement, a desk clock showing three in the afternoon and a key ring. Image · AI illustration](/assets/img/articles/bok-325-loan-reset-date-dec15-2026.jpg)

## Five votes, and one changed sentence

The vote was 5 to 2. Members Hwang Kun-il and Lee Soo-hyung argued for holding at 3.00%. The decision cited two numbers, growth and prices. The 2026 growth forecast rose to 3.9% from 3.3% and the 2027 forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%. Consumer inflation was held at 2.7% this year and raised to 2.4% from 2.3% next year. Core inflation rose to 2.6% for both years from 2.5%. In October consumer and core prices both ran at 2.8%, above the 2.0% target.

One sentence changed too. The October statement said the committee would decide "the timing and pace of further increases"; this time "pace" is gone, leaving "the timing of further increases." Governor Hyun Song Shin said of the dot plot, "read it as it is." Of the 21 dots for six months out, in May next year, eight sit at 3.50%, seven at 3.75% and six at today's 3.25%. Fifteen of the 21 are above the current rate, and the median rose to 3.50% from 3.25% in August.

## It had already reached the bank counter

What moved before the policy rate was the banks' cost of funds. COFIX, the benchmark for variable-rate mortgages, rose to 3.62% for October from 3.18% in August, up 0.44 percentage points in two months and the highest since February 2024. COFIX is the weighted average rate banks pay for money raised through deposits and bank bonds. When banks raise deposit rates the index follows, and that cost is added to loan rates. Market rates actually fell slightly in October; rising time-deposit rates pushed the index up.

Some numbers have already risen. The average rate on new mortgage loans in October was 4.98%, the highest since March 2012. KB Kookmin Bank raised its six-month variable mortgage rate to 4.85-6.25% from Nov 17, and Woori Bank to 5.04-6.24%. As of Nov 26 the five major banks' variable rates run 4.52-6.59% and five-year fixed rates 4.33-6.30%. The floor of the variable range is already above the floor of the fixed range.

## December 15, 3 p.m.

COFIX for the previous month is published at 3 p.m. on the 15th, or on the next business day if the 15th is a holiday. That is why October's figure came a day late, on Nov 16, and November's will be published on Dec 15. Banks apply the new figure to new loans from the next business day; for loans already drawn, the rate is recalculated with the figure published just before each reset date set in the contract, every 3, 6 or 12 months. On a six-month cycle, several disclosures can pass before the next reset without changing anything.

There is more than one benchmark, either. For October, new-business COFIX was 3.62%, the balance-based index 3.26% and the new-balance index 2.93%. Two borrowers at the same bank on the same day can see benchmark rates 0.69 percentage points apart depending on which index the contract names, which is 2.07 million won a year on a 300 million won loan. The new-business index is the one that follows rates upward fastest.

> "The rate on a loan already drawn is adjusted to reflect the change in the benchmark when the rate reset cycle comes due" — Korea Federation of Banks, Understanding Loan Rates

## The people who chose variable in July

The arithmetic is simple. On a 300 million won balance at 5.0%, interest is 15 million won a year, or 1.25 million won a month. Add the full 0.25 percentage points and it becomes 15.75 million won a year and 1,312,500 won a month: 62,500 won more a month, 750,000 won a year. On 500 million won it is 1.25 million won a year. With three increases this year, in July, August and today, the cumulative move is 0.75 percentage points, so on the same 300 million won an interest-only borrower pays 2.25 million won a year, 187,500 won a month, more than in June. If the rate reaches the dot-plot median of 3.50%, it becomes 3 million won and 250,000 won. On a 30-year equal-instalment repayment (300 million won, 4.90% to 5.15%) the first monthly payment rises to 1,638,079 won from 1,592,180 won, or 45,899 won. The same increase feels different depending on how the loan is repaid.

A cheaper fixed rate does not make refinancing right by itself. Early-repayment fees, the conditions attached to preferential rates and the rate applied once the fixed period ends all have to be compared before the real saving appears.

## Check the date first

The next meeting is next year. Governor Shin said consumer inflation will reach the target only in 2028, and that for vulnerable borrowers "the most appropriate response is financial policy accompanied by fiscal support." Markets mostly see a terminal rate of 3.50%. If you have a loan or are about to take one, check the benchmark named in the contract, the reset cycle and the next reset date. Today's announcement arrives on that date.

factCheck.title: Fact check & calculation basis
factCheck.note: Interest rates and forecasts are the Bank of Korea's monetary policy direction press release on November 26, 2026 and the revised economic outlook, and growth rates and prices are forecasts (not confirmed results). COFIX 3.62% is the value announced on November 16th for handling in October 2026, and the value for November is scheduled to be announced on December 15th. The interest amount in the text (300 million won, 5.0% per year, 750,000 won per year, 62,500 won per month per 0.25% point, 2.25 million won per year for a cumulative 0.75% point, 1.25 million won per year for 500 million won) is a simple calculation assuming that the balance and interest rate remain the same and the increase is fully reflected in the loan interest rate. In reality, the base rate increase is based on the COFIX, additional interest rate, and preferential interest rate. The scope and perspective change as you go through it. The 30-year equal repayment amount of principal and interest is 300 million won, a self-calculated value calculated with monthly compound interest of 4.90% and 5.15% per year (1,592,180 won, 1,638,079 won). The variable and fixed interest rates of the five major banks range from the lowest to the highest for each product at the time of reporting on November 26 and vary depending on the borrower's conditions. The dot plot is a conditional forecast after 6 months and is not a confirmed interest rate path. The 300 million won interest calculation was based on the condition that the principal was not repaid.

title: Section 301 Overcapacity Tariffs: What the 14-Economy Rate Card Adds, and Where It Does Not
deck: USTR named 14 economies that supplied about 60% of US goods imports in 2025 and floated duties from 10% to 40%. The 'net of' clauses, the exemptions and one hearing in January decide what any importer actually pays.
author: Insight Brief Desk
summary: USTR determined on 25 November 2026 that 14 economies — China, the EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Singapore, India, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia and Bangladesh — maintain structural excess capacity in manufacturing, and proposed duties of up to 40%. Mexico and Norway are still under investigation; Mexico alone supplied $534.3bn of US goods imports in 2025.

None of the rates is in force: comments close on 5 January 2027 and the Section 301 Committee hearing opens on 25 January 2027. Read against the duties in force since July, the proposal adds 2.5 to 8 percentage points for most partners that hold trade agreements and 7.5 to 15 for those that do not — but China's 20% stacks on the 25% first-term tariffs for roughly 45%, rising to about 65% if the 10 January truce lapses.

Exemptions for Section 232 goods (steel, aluminium, copper, vehicles, wood, patented pharmaceuticals, semiconductors) and a no-stacking rule cut the taxed base well below the $2.07tn the 14 economies supplied in 2025. Yale Budget Lab estimates the average statutory rate would rise from 11.4% to about 13.9%, close to the 13.8% of February 2026.
body:
On 25 November the Office of the US Trade Representative published a finding eight months in the making: 14 economies, from China and the European Union to Cambodia and Bangladesh, maintain policies that create structural excess capacity in manufacturing, and those policies are unreasonable and burden US commerce. Under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act of 1974, that makes them actionable.

What followed was a rate card, and most coverage stopped there. China up to 20%. Vietnam up to 35%. India up to 25%. Five Southeast Asian garment and electronics producers up to 18%. Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and the EU at 15%. All of it "up to", none of it in force, and none of it due to reach a customs entry before the end of January.

Three details decide what an importer actually pays: the words "net of", the exemption annexes, and whether a trade agreement holds.

## The investigation behind the number

USTR opened the investigation on 11 March 2026 against 16 economies (91 Fed. Reg. 12886), took more than 1,070 written comments and held four days of hearings in May with nearly 140 witnesses.

Two of the 16 dropped out of Wednesday's determination: Mexico and Norway, both still under investigation. That is not a small omission. Mexico supplied $534.3 billion of US goods imports in 2025, more than any other country and 15.6% of the total, and for now faces none of this action.

![Containers wait at a US port at dawn. The proposed duties would fall on apparel, furniture, appliances, auto parts and machinery — the goods that fill a container and a shopping cart.](assets/img/articles/section-301-overcapacity-tariffs-14-economies-2027.jpg)

## What is still only a proposal

The determination is final; the duties are not. Written comments and requests to appear are due by 5 January 2027 (dockets USTR–2026–0278 and USTR–2026–0741), and the Section 301 Committee hears testimony at the US International Trade Commission from 10 a.m. on 25 January 2027. No effective date has been announced. The July round shows the pattern: duties apply to goods entered after a stated minute, with a four-day in-transit window for cargo already loaded.

## The rate card, economy by economy

- **China**: up to 20%, net of the duty it already pays under the forced-labor Section 301 action. Annex A goods would pay up to 10%, and Annex B goods — the Board of Trade's "30-for-30" list of products recommended for tariff relief, about $30 billion of imports — are exempt. If USTR judges engagement inadequate, up to 40%.
- **European Union**: 15% on all goods, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 duties. Up to 20% if commitments fall short.
- **Japan, Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan**: 15%, net of MFN and existing Section 301. Fallbacks are 20% for Japan and Switzerland, 25% for Korea and Taiwan.
- **Singapore**: up to 20%; 10% if it concludes a reciprocal trade agreement.
- **Vietnam**: up to 35%; 20% with an agreement.
- **India**: up to 25%; 17% with an agreement.
- **Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand**: up to 18%. The fallback is 20% for Bangladesh and 25% for the other four.

## Where "net of" changes the answer

The phrase sounds like housekeeping. It is the difference between two very different tariffs.

For the EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland, the quoted rate is a ceiling on the most-favoured-nation duty and the Section 301 duty combined: an EU good with a 4.5% MFN rate gets a 10.5% Section 301 duty and pays 15% in total. For the other eight, the rate is net of existing Section 301 duties only, so MFN stacks on top: a Vietnamese good with a 3.2% MFN rate pays 3.2% plus 20%, not 20%.

Measured against the duties in force since 24 July 2026 — the forced-labor Section 301 rates of a flat 10%, or 10% and 12.5% net of MFN — the proposal moves each partner by a different amount. These are Insight Brief calculations and assume the proposed rate is applied in full:

- **Singapore**: −2.5 percentage points if the 10% agreement rate applies. A proposal that can cut a duty.
- **Korea, Japan, Switzerland**: +2.5 points.
- **EU, Taiwan**: +5 points.
- **Thailand**: +5.5 points.
- **China, Vietnam**: +7.5 points, and far more if the fallback binds — +27.5 for China, +22.5 for Vietnam.
- **Indonesia, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Cambodia**: +8 points.
- **India**: +15 points without an agreement, +7 with one.

China is the one place where the new duty stacks on an older one. The 25% Section 301 tariffs of Trump's first term stay, so the 20% would bring the combined rate to roughly 45%. That 20% is also the rate written into the Kuala Lumpur arrangement of 30 October 2025, whose truce expires on 10 January 2027, two weeks before the hearing. If it lapses and USTR moves to 40%, the combined rate would be about 65%.

## What the duties will not touch

Except for China, the notices propose to exempt goods already covered by Section 232 national security duties — steel, aluminium and copper articles, vehicles and parts, wood products, patented pharmaceuticals and semiconductors — and the new duties do not stack on the forced-labor Section 301 rates. "These are not really additive," USTR's Jamieson Greer told CNBC, describing the total change as one that "really will just top up a few percentage points."

Those carve-outs change which economies are really exposed. The 14 supplied about $2.07 trillion of America's $3.41 trillion in goods imports in 2025, roughly 60% — but semiconductors, a large share of Taiwan's $201.4 billion, are out, and so are patented pharmaceuticals. What remains is apparel, footwear, furniture, toys, appliances, auto parts and machinery.

## Back to February

The Yale Budget Lab put the aggregate in one line: the average statutory tariff rate would rise from 11.4% to about 13.9% early next year, against 13.8% in February, before the Supreme Court struck down the emergency-law tariffs this system replaced. The administration said it wanted to rebuild the IEEPA regime using Section 301, the lab noted, "and with this proposal, it will have done so in the aggregate."

Not everyone reads it the same way. Capital Economics' Stephen Brown called the announcement "not as alarming as it looks", pointing to the exemptions, the smaller increases for partners that hold agreements and the no-stacking rule, while still expecting a marginal push to prices. The Budget Lab puts the cost to households under current law at about $900 a year, and about 0.7% on consumer prices.

> "It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind." — ING analysts, 25 November 2026

## Why the politics did not stop it

Republicans lost the midterm elections, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote found 62% of respondents backed Democratic efforts to repeal the tariffs. Legal durability is why the wall survived anyway: the Supreme Court closed the IEEPA route, not the tariff authority, and Section 301 requires an investigation, findings and a comment period, all of which this action has. Undoing it would also mean unpicking the trade agreements that set the caps, which is why Nathaniel Halvorson, a former USTR official now at Baker McKenzie, expects bipartisan reluctance.

## The dates that matter

- **5 January 2027**: written comments and hearing requests close.
- **10 January 2027**: the truce that fixes China's 20% lapses.
- **25 January 2027**: the Section 301 Committee hearing opens at the USITC.
- **Undated**: determinations for Mexico, the largest source of US imports at $534.3 billion in 2025, and for Norway.

title: 97.8% and 63.0% — the AI that gets it right once and the AI that gets it right sixteen times
deck: Google DeepMind published Humanity's First Exam (HFE) on Kaggle on November 24, 2026: 544 prompts about counting and reading, not hard problems, grouped into 136 families. The top five models score 96% to 98% on a single attempt, but under a rule that needs all sixteen attempts in a family to be right they average 85.8%. The gap runs from 7.6 to 80.1 points, and no Korean model is on the board.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: HFE, published by Google DeepMind on Kaggle on November 24, 2026, puts 544 basic prompts (316 of them with an image) into 136 families and answers every prompt six times, so a family passes only when all sixteen attempts are correct. It is not a harder test but a test of whether a model is right every time.

Across 58,752 rollouts from 18 models, the top five scored 96% to 98% on single attempts and got at least one of sixteen right in every family, yet their family pass⁴ averages 85.8%. GPT-6.2 Astra leads at 92.4% and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite trails at 18.6%, a gap of up to 80.1 points.

73% of wrong answers were visual perception errors. 112 prompts (28 families) are open under CC-BY-4.0, the other 432 are held out, and the Kaggle competition runs through December 15, 2026. Neither the 16-model leaderboard nor the 18-model paper includes a Korean model.
body:
On November 24, 2026, Google DeepMind posted Humanity's First Exam (HFE) on Kaggle. It is not hard maths or coding. One prompt asks how many coffee mugs in a photo have no steam rising from them. Its 544 prompts sit in 136 'families' across 20 foundational capabilities, and 316 of them (58.1%) come with an image.

![An examination hall of sixteen desks in a row, the answer sheet on the last one crumpled and dropped on the floor](/assets/img/articles/hfe-reliability-floor-544-2026.jpg)

## Fail once in sixteen and the family scores zero

A family is one newly written seed prompt and three variants. The variants change object names, clause order and image layout while the logic stays and only the answer moves. Each prompt is answered six times independently, and the score is the chance that four drawn from those six are all correct: 1.0 for six out of six, 0.333 for five, 0.067 for four, zero for three or fewer. Multiplying the four prompt scores across the family gives family pass⁴, and only sixteen correct attempts out of sixteen earn a point. A seed survived only if at least three of four people solved it without tools (single-rater accuracy 90.8%, median solve one minute).

## Where 6.6 points becomes 29.4

The paper had 18 models answer 58,752 times. The top five scored 96% to 98% on single attempts, and in every family at least one of sixteen attempts was right — 100%. Yet the share of families with all sixteen correct averages 85.8%. The best, GPT-6.2 Astra, reaches 92.4%, then Gemini 4 Neon at 85.8%, and the lowest, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, 18.6%. The gap between the capability ceiling and the reliability floor runs from 7.6 points to 80.1 points.

> "Real-world deployment requires evaluations that enable us to measure and raise the reliability floor, not just the capability ceiling." — Google DeepMind, HFE technical report, November 24, 2026

Repetition amplifies the difference. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 91.2% on a single attempt, only 6.6 points below Astra's 97.8%, but its family pass⁴ is 63.0% against 92.4% — a 29.4-point gap. Among families that fail, 61% to 85% got exactly one prompt wrong. The failure is not a missing capability but the inability to do the same thing the same way every time.

## The failures are in the eyes

Of 5,823 failed rollouts, 95% were wrong answers, and 73% of those were visual perception errors: misreading a position, direction or path in 31%, miscounting objects in 23%. Forty percent were off by a single element and 16% involved objects partly hidden or overlapping. The top nine models score 83% to 97% on text families but fall to 64% to 89% once an image is attached, and more thinking time barely fills the hole: dropping Gemini 4 Carbon from high to low effort costs 42.4 points on maths and algorithms (97.5% to 55.1%) but only 3.1 points on vision. Humans and models also rank the difficulty in opposite order (Spearman -0.64).

## A refusal counts as a wrong answer

Wrong answers are not the only failures: 3% were refusals, 2% hit the output limit and 0.1% were harness errors. Every refusal came from Anthropic models. Opus 5.5 refused 1.6% of the time, and that alone took it from 67.4% to 63.0% — safety alignment billed as a score. Grading fell to Gemini 3.1 Pro, and with Google models on the same board the paper names that as a limitation; a re-grade of 1,492 failed pairs by Claude Fable 5.2 agreed on the cause 84% of the time (κ=0.81). The Kaggle leaderboard (16 models) and the paper (18) are separate runs, so the top score differs too: 90.7% and 92.4%.

## In Korea, the forms still have no such column

No Korean model is on the board: all 16 on the leaderboard and all 18 in the paper come from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. Korea's certification axis runs elsewhere. The AI Trustworthiness Certification (CAT) that the Telecommunications Technology Association (TTA) has run since December 2023 audits conformity with ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, TR 24028 and 38507 — all management-system, risk and governance standards, with no test method for whether an output is right every time. The KOLAS accreditation the Jeonju Information & Culture Industry Promotion Agency won on November 23 (ISO/IEC 4213, classification performance) measures accuracy once. Robustness (TR 24029) and data quality (ISO/IEC 5259) are planned additions; repeat consistency is not on the list.

So the only open tool in Korea for checking 'sixteen out of sixteen' is this exam. 112 prompts (28 families) are published under CC-BY-4.0, chosen for a 0.97 rank correlation with the full set, and the other 432 stay private. Apply the same rule — six draws per prompt, three variants, all sixteen — to your own model or retrieval-augmented pipeline, and procurement gets a second number to ask for.

## December 15

Kaggle is running a three-week competition through December 15 for everyday questions that models still get wrong. Accepted prompts are cited in the next paper and the prizes are $50,000 worth of swag. DeepMind says frontier models have climbed far on this exam in six months. Yesterday's ceiling becomes today's floor, and the exam has to be rewritten at that speed.

The question this table answers is not 'can it work' but 'does it work every time'. The moment a model goes into repeat work, a 97.8% single-attempt score becomes advertising and sixteen becomes the contract term.

factCheck.title: Fact check & sources
factCheck.note: 'Sixteen' unpacks the rule: each prompt is answered six times, the prompt score is the chance that four drawn without replacement are all correct, and the four prompt scores are multiplied across the family. A family actually draws 24 answers (4 prompts x 6), and a prompt scores 1.0 only when six of six are right. The 85.8% average is the paper's figure for the top five models; across all 18 the range is 18.6% to 92.4%. The same material carries two boards: the paper's 18 models put GPT-6.2 Astra first at 92.4%, the Kaggle leaderboard's 16 models put it at 90.7% in an isolated environment, so this article quotes the paper and notes the leaderboard difference separately. The 90.8% human figure is single-rater accuracy on the 136 final seed prompts (494/544); the paper gives no human score on the variants or under the family rule. The prompts were adversarially filtered to expose model blind spots and many images are synthetic, so the paper itself says the scores are not an estimate of everyday failure rates. Grading was done by one model, Gemini 3.1 Pro (a cross-provider audit agreed on cause in 84% of cases, κ=0.81, and 3% of wrong rollouts were flagged as possibly defensible), and refusals, empty outputs and output-limit truncations all score zero; Opus 5.5's 4.4-point drop is what counting refusals as correct would recover. 'No Korean model' comes from reading the 16-row leaderboard and the 18-model table directly. The Korean comparison rests on TTA's published CAT overview and its list of ISO/IEC standards; the full CAT test items are not published on that page, so the point is that no repeat-consistency axis appears in the published criteria, not that none exists. The KOLAS scope for Jeonju is as reported by Electronic Times; the accreditation certificate itself was not examined. The Kaggle prize is 'a share of $50k in swag' as stated on the leaderboard page.

title: Iron ore is at $86.9, a four-year low — but coking coal at $273 is what pushed the blast furnace's raw-material bill back up
deck: On 17 November Singapore iron ore fell to $86.9 a tonne, its lowest in almost four years. Chinese ports hold 153.75 million tonnes, only 10% of blast furnaces are profitable, and Guinea has overtaken South Africa and Canada as the third-largest exporter. Yet POSCO's third-quarter iron ore price fell 11% to $85 while coking coal rose 4% to $248. The benchmark being negotiated for 2027 is the same one Korean blast furnaces price against.
author: Insight Brief Editorial Room
summary: Singapore's December iron ore contract hit $86.9 a tonne on 17 November, its lowest in almost four years, and Dalian's main contract closed at 654 yuan ($98.02) on 23 November. Stock at China's 35 ports rose for a fourth week to 153.75 million tonnes, and only 10% of steelmakers were profitable, down from 38% a year earlier.

Guinea shipped more than 5 million tonnes in October, overtaking South Africa and Canada to rank third behind Australia and Brazil. Its 22 million tonnes this year already exceed the initial 20 million tonne forecast, and Simandou's second production line at the northern mine started up in early November.

Korea's raw-material bill runs on two tracks. POSCO's third-quarter iron ore price fell 11% to $85 a tonne while coking coal rose 4% to $248, and in won coking coal gained 27.6%, offsetting the fall in ore. The benchmark CMRG is negotiating for 2027 is also the one Korean blast furnaces price against.
body:
On 17 November 2026 the December iron ore contract on the Singapore Exchange fell to $86.9 a tonne, its lowest in almost four years. Six days later, on 23 November, the main Dalian contract closed at 654 yuan ($98.02) and the Singapore December contract tried to rebound at $88.85. Over the same period imported iron ore stock at China's 35 ports rose for a fourth straight week to 153.75 million tonnes. Steel demand explains both why the price fell and why the ore is piling up.

![The iron ore yard at a steelworks port at winter dawn: red-brown ore piles and a stacker-reclaimer, a bulk carrier at the berth, a blast furnace beyond the haze. Image · AI illustration](/assets/img/articles/iron-ore-four-year-low-coking-coal-2026.jpg)

## Only 10% of blast furnaces are making money

As of 19 November average daily hot metal output in China was 2.3 million tonnes, an eight-month low and a sixth consecutive weekly decline. Only 10% of steelmakers were operating at a profit, down from 38% a year earlier (Mysteel data, cited by Reuters on 23 November). China's October crude steel output was 70.83 million tonnes, the lowest since March. Iron ore imports moved the other way: 1.06055 billion tonnes in January-October, up 3.1% on a year earlier (China customs). The stockpile is not growing because more ore is arriving. Average daily port outbound volume fell for a fourth week to 3.0 million tonnes, 210,000 tonnes below the level of 23 October.

## The month Guinea became the world's third-largest exporter

Last month Guinea shipped more than 5 million tonnes of iron ore, overtaking South Africa and Canada for 3% of global seaborne trade. Its shipments this year have passed 22 million tonnes, already above the 20 million tonnes forecast for all of 2026. The Simandou project exported 8.9 million tonnes in the third quarter, up from 6 million in the previous three months: 6.55 million tonnes from Baowu-Winning and 2.16 million from SimFer, the Rio Tinto and Chalco joint venture. In early November the second production line at the northern mine started up, and SimFer's 2027 sales forecast stands at 26.99 million tonnes (analyst average). Its dedicated southern port targets start-up in the first quarter of 2027. The 650 km railway and the port can move 72 million tonnes a year today.

## When the price splits in two

The raw material cost of a Korean blast furnace is set by two numbers. Iron ore that POSCO bought in the third quarter cost $85 a tonne, down 11% from $95 in the previous quarter. Coking coal rose 4% to $248. Quarterly averages in 2025 ran between $184 and $200, so coal is up roughly 30% in a year. In won, ore cost 131,000 won a tonne and coal 342,000 won. Coking coal is up 27.6% from 268,000 won in 2025, while iron ore is down 1.5% from 133,000 won (POSCO Holdings third-quarter report).

> "Iron ore: based on the Platts assessment (62% Fe CFR China) minus the Australia-China seaborne freight (C5)." — POSCO Holdings, third-quarter 2026 report, basis for raw material prices

That benchmark is being pulled at right now. China's state purchasing body CMRG signed a supply contract with Rio Tinto in October, and Fortescue said on 22 October that its operations could be affected if talks with CMRG are not settled by the end of the year. The dispute with BHP ended in April with BHP accepting several indices and a small discount. Korean mills also price ore at China CFR minus freight, so the outcome of that negotiation lands directly on the domestic cost sheet.

## Why coking coal will not come down

Australian premium low-vol hard coking coal was $273.60 a tonne on 18 November. It peaked at $284.90 on 10 September, a two-and-a-half-year high, and has only corrected since. Mines idled by safety inspections after the May accident in Shanxi numbered 49 on 23 November, up from 41 a week earlier (Mysteel). On 25 November Chinese coking coal and coke futures jumped 4.7% to a one-month high. China's coal imports from Australia reached 9.92 million tonnes in October, the most since April 2020, and coking coal accounted for 70% of the year-on-year increase.

## What is left for the fourth quarter and 2027

POSCO reported 455 billion won of standalone operating profit in the third quarter, up 66.1% from the previous quarter, but higher raw material costs cut 214 billion won, and price increases worth 180 billion won plus 159 billion won of cost savings filled the gap. In the fourth quarter a revamp of Gwangyang's No. 2 blast furnace will cut output by 920,000 tonnes and sales by 570,000 tonnes. Raw materials look friendlier: Hana Securities expects lower ore prices and the exchange rate to feed into input costs alongside automotive price increases, and Hanwha Investment & Securities sees blast furnace raw material costs falling 14% in 2027 from this year. Korea imports all of its iron ore, and nearly half of the 70 million tonnes a year enters through Gwangyang. Australia supplies 70% of POSCO's raw materials. With the price at a four-year low, what pushes Korean costs back up is the coking coal on the same ship and the terms of the 2027 contracts.
